## Statement

For $d\in\{1,2\}$, suppose a countably additive measure $\lambda_d$ on $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ is supplied and satisfies
$$\lambda_d\!\left(\prod_{j=1}^d(a_j,b_j]\right)=\prod_{j=1}^d(b_j-a_j)\qquad(a_j<b_j).$$
No assertion about constructing these measures is made.

1. If $Q$ is a nondegenerate compact box and $h:Q\to\mathbb R$ is bounded, Borel measurable and Riemann integrable, then its integral against the supplied measure equals its proper Riemann integral. Nonnegative Borel functions on the whole space are computed from increasing compact-box cutoffs by monotone convergence.
2. For the supplied $\lambda_1$, every $m\in\mathbb R$, $v>0$ and
$$g_{m,v}(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi v}}e^{-(x-m)^2/(2v)}$$
satisfy
$$\int g_{m,v}\,d\lambda_1=1,\qquad \int xg_{m,v}(x)\,d\lambda_1(x)=m,\qquad \int(x-m)^2g_{m,v}(x)\,d\lambda_1(x)=v.$$
The signed first moment is absolutely integrable. These are density-integral statements and require no choice axiom in addition to the supplied measures.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The supplied Borel measures and their half-open-box volumes in the Statement.

[F1] Borel sets form the sigma-algebra generated by open sets. A continuous real function is Borel measurable: its inverse images of open sets are open, and the sets whose inverse images are Borel form a sigma-algebra. [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]

[F2] Measures are monotone; nonnegative simple integrals are finite sums of coefficients times cell measures and agree with the nonnegative integral. [[prop-measure-monotonicity]], [[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]], [[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]

[F3] Nonnegative integrals are monotone and homogeneous, and integrals are linear on absolutely integrable functions. [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-lebesgue-integral-on-l-one]]

[F4] A bounded Riemann integrand has equal upper and lower Darboux integrals; continuous one-variable functions on compact intervals are Riemann integrable. [[thm-multidimensional-darboux-equals-riemann]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]

[F5] Monotone convergence and dominated convergence apply on a supplied measure space. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[thm-dominated-convergence]]

[F6] The improper Riemann Gaussian integral is $\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-t^2}dt=\sqrt\pi$; proper substitution and integration by parts hold on compact intervals. [[thm-gaussian-integral]], [[thm-substitution]], [[thm-integration-by-parts]]

[F7] The exponential is continuously differentiable with derivative itself, and the chain rule applies. Exponential growth dominates each fixed polynomial, and a positive real has a positive square root. [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]

## Proof

**Proof technique:** finite Darboux bounds followed by explicit cutoffs.

1.1 Every compact box has finite supplied measure, since it is contained in a larger half-open box. A bounded coordinate face has measure zero: enclose it in a half-open slab of arbitrary positive thickness $\eta$, with the other side lengths fixed and positive. Its measure is at most $C\eta$ by the given volume formula and [F2], and so must be zero. In dimension one this says that singletons are null. Consequently compact boxes have their usual volumes, and disjointifying a finite grid of closed cells only removes null faces. [given, F2, algebra]

1.2 For a nonnegative bounded Borel Riemann integrand $h$ on $Q$, take the infimum and supremum of $h$ on each cell of any finite grid. The corresponding disjoint-cell simple functions bound $h$, and [F2] and step 1.1 make their integrals exactly the lower and upper Darboux sums. By [F3] and [F4], the integral of $h$ is squeezed to its Riemann value. For signed bounded $h$, add a finite constant to make it nonnegative and subtract that constant's finite integral using [F3]. This proves the compact comparison. For nonnegative Borel $H$ on the whole space, $H\mathbf1_{[-n,n]^d}\uparrow H$, so [F5] gives the cutoff assertion. The grids, extrema, and cutoff sequence are finite or explicitly specified; no countable selection is used. [step 1.1, F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

2.1 Put $\phi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. It is continuous and Borel by [F1] and [F7]. On $[-n,n]$, proper substitution $t=\sqrt2u$ in [F6] computes its Riemann integral. As $n\to\infty$, [F6]'s improper Gaussian value makes this tend to one. Step 1.2 identifies each compact integral with its supplied-measure integral, and [F5] gives $\int\phi\,d\lambda_1=1$. [F1, F4, F5, F6, F7, step 1.2]

2.2 Since $\phi'=-t\phi$ by [F7], compact integration by parts [F6] gives
$$\int_{-n}^nt^2\phi(t)dt=\int_{-n}^n\phi(t)dt-2n\phi(n).$$
All functions and derivatives here are continuous, so the proper integral hypotheses hold by [F4]. Also $n\phi(n)\to0$: for $n\ge1$, $n^2/2\ge n/2$, hence $0\le ne^{-n^2/2}\le ne^{-n/2}\to0$ by [F7]. Apply step 1.2 and monotone convergence [F5] to the nonnegative $t^2\phi(t)$ cutoffs. Step 2.1 then gives $\int t^2\phi(t)\,d\lambda_1=1$. [F4, F5, F6, F7, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

2.3 The bound $|t|\le1+t^2$ and steps 2.1–2.2 make $|t|\phi(t)$ integrable. On each symmetric compact interval, the Riemann integral of $t\phi(t)$ is zero by oddness, using the proper substitution $t=-u$. Step 1.2 transfers these compact integrals to the supplied measure. Dominated convergence [F5], with majorant $|t|\phi(t)$, yields $\int t\phi(t)\,d\lambda_1=0$. [F3, F5, F6, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

3.1 Fix $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma=\sqrt v>0$. On the explicitly specified intervals $[m-\sigma n,m+\sigma n]$, proper substitution $x=m+\sigma t$ gives compact integrals of $g_{m,v}$, $(x-m)^2g_{m,v}$ and $(x-m)g_{m,v}$ equal to the corresponding integrals of $\phi$, $\sigma^2t^2\phi$ and $\sigma t\phi$ on $[-n,n]$. Step 1.2 and monotone convergence give mass one and centered second moment $\sigma^2=v$. Since $|x-m|\le1+(x-m)^2$, the centered first moment is absolutely integrable, and the same dominated-cutoff argument as step 2.3 gives centered mean zero. Linearity then gives raw mean $m$. This proves both claims for the supplied measures without constructing any new measure or invoking a choice-dependent normal-law supplier. [F3, F5, F6, F7, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

Optimizing an independent Gaussian mean-field family by the evidence lower bound need not recover the marginal variances or dependence structure of the exact inferential target.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The reference area measure $\lambda_2$ is supplied, as in the example's Lebesgue integration setting. Its Borel restriction has the half-open rectangle volume formula. Define $\lambda_1(A)=\lambda_2(A\times(0,1])$ for Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R$; this supplies the needed length measure without an existence or completion construction. On $\mathbb R^2$ with the supplied area measure, put $\beta=3/4$ and define the target density
$$\gamma(x,y)=\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt\beta}\exp\!\left(-\frac{x^2-xy+y^2}{2\beta}\right).$$
This target is an exact inferential target by taking prior density $\gamma$, the sample space $\{\star\}$ with $P_\theta(\{\star\})=1$ for every $\theta$, and likelihood version $\ell_\star\equiv1$. The variational family consists of independent Gaussian factors
$$q(x,y)=g_{m_1,v_1}(x)g_{m_2,v_2}(y),\quad m_j\in\mathbb R,\ v_j>0,\qquad g_{m,v}(z)=(2\pi v)^{-1/2}e^{-(z-m)^2/(2v)}.$$

[F1] A fixed measurable likelihood and positive finite evidence define the exact target; the displayed target density is its prior density when the likelihood is identically one. [[def-exact-inferential-target-and-approximation-chain]]

[F2] ELBO admissibility requires support on the target support and finite log integrals, and $\operatorname{ELBO}(q)=\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu$. [[def-variational-family-and-elbo]]

[F3] Under the supplied length/area measures' box-volume contract, compact bounded Borel Riemann integrals equal the corresponding measure integrals, and the density $g_{m,v}$ has mass one, mean $m$, and variance $v$. The proof uses explicit cutoffs and finite integration by parts and assumes no choice axiom. [[lem-gaussian-density-integrals-for-supplied-length-measures]]

[F4] Tonelli applies to nonnegative product-measurable functions on sigma-finite product spaces. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

[F5] Absolutely integrable functions on sigma-finite product spaces may be integrated in either order. [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

[F6] A nonnegative measurable density defines a measure, which is a probability when its total mass is one. Integrating against that density measure agrees with integrating the product against the base measure. [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]], [[thm-integration-against-a-density]]

[F7] Sigma-finite factors have a product measure with the rectangle formula. Measures agreeing on a generating pi-system and its increasing finite-mass exhaustion agree everywhere. Rational half-open boxes generate the Euclidean Borel sigma-algebra. [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], [[thm-measure-uniqueness-on-a-sigma-finite-pi-system]], [[thm-rational-box-generators-of-the-borel-sigma-algebra-on-rn]]

[F8] $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$. [[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]]

## Counterexample

**Given:** The supplied reference measures and explicit target and variational densities above.

1.1 Let $\rho=1/2$, so $\beta=1-\rho^2=3/4$, and write $\phi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. Countable additivity of the supplied area measure makes $A\mapsto\lambda_2(A\times(0,1])$ a Borel measure, with $\lambda_1((a,b])=b-a$ by rectangle volume. The explicit intervals $(-n,n]$ exhaust $\mathbb R$ and have supplied measure $2n$, so the factor measure is sigma-finite. Its product exists by [F7]. It and the supplied $\lambda_2$ agree on half-open boxes by the volume formula and on the finite-mass exhaustion $(-n,n]^2$; [F7] and [F8] identify their Borel measures. All displayed densities and polynomial moment integrands are continuous and hence Borel: inverse images of open sets are open, and inverse-image preservation of sigma-algebra operations gives the Borel assertion. Thus [F8] makes them product-measurable. The compact comparison and Gaussian integral statements in [F3] now apply to these supplied measures. Direct algebra gives $\gamma(x,y)=\phi(x)g_{\rho x,\beta}(y)=\phi(y)g_{\rho y,\beta}(x)$. Each inner Gaussian density has mass one by [F3], so Tonelli [F4] proves that $\gamma$ has mass one and both marginals $\phi$. By [F3] and density integration [F6], the marginal means are zero and second moments are one. Since $|xy|\le(x^2+y^2)/2$, the cross moment is absolutely integrable. Fubini [F5], [F6] and the mean of $g_{\rho x,\beta}$ in [F3] give $E[XY]=\int x\phi(x)\rho x\,dx=\rho$. Thus the target has marginal variances $1$ and covariance $1/2$. With likelihood one the evidence is $1$, so [F1] identifies $\gamma$ as the exact target. [F1, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

1.2 For $m_j\in\mathbb R$ and $v_j>0$, [F3] supplies the normalized Lebesgue densities $g_{m_j,v_j}$ and their means $m_j$ and variances $v_j$. Tonelli [F4] gives total mass one for $q$. The logarithms of $\gamma$ and $q$ are quadratic; the finite second moments and $|xy|\le(x^2+y^2)/2$ make their absolute values integrable under $q$. Both densities are everywhere positive, so $q$ is admissible by [F2]. Fubini [F5] and [F6] give $E_q[X^2]=m_1^2+v_1$, $E_q[Y^2]=m_2^2+v_2$, and $E_q[XY]=m_1m_2$. [F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 One has $\log\gamma=-\log(2\pi\sqrt\beta)-(x^2-xy+y^2)/(2\beta)$ and $-E_{g_{m_j,v_j}}\log g_{m_j,v_j}=\tfrac12\log(2\pi v_j)+\tfrac12$, using the mean and variance in step 1.2. Substituting these expressions and the second moments from step 1.2 into [F2] yields $\operatorname{ELBO}(q)=C-\frac{m_1^2-m_1m_2+m_2^2+v_1+v_2}{2\beta}+\frac12\log v_1+\frac12\log v_2$, where $C$ is independent of $(m_1,m_2,v_1,v_2)$. The mean quadratic equals $(m_1-\rho m_2)^2+\beta m_2^2$, so its unique minimum and the ELBO-maximizing means are $m_1=m_2=0$. [F2, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 For either variance the variable part is $r(v)=-v/(2\beta)+\tfrac12\log v$, with derivative $r'(v)=(\beta-v)/(2\beta v)$. It is positive on $(0,\beta)$ and negative on $(\beta,\infty)$, so the unique maximum is $v=\beta=3/4$. The target variance is $1$ and covariance is $1/2$ by step 1.1, whereas the optimizing independent factors have variance $3/4$ and covariance $0$ by step 1.2. Thus the unique ELBO optimizer differs from the exact target. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let
$$I:=\int_{\mathbb R} e^{-x^2}\,dx.$$
Then $I=\sqrt{\pi}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The nonnegative function $x \mapsto e^{-x^2}$ and the supplied reference length measure $\lambda_1$, whose Borel restriction is countably additive and agrees with half-open interval lengths. The plane measure used below is its product; no construction of Lebesgue length measure or its completion is used.

[L1] Tonelli applies to nonnegative product-measurable functions on sigma-finite measure spaces. ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])

[L2] The nonnegative improper plane Gaussian integral equals $\pi$. ([[lem-plane-gaussian-integral-in-polar-coordinates]])

[L3] Sigma-finite factors have a product measure with the rectangle formula. Measures agreeing on a generating pi-system with a common finite-mass exhaustion agree everywhere; rational half-open boxes generate the Euclidean Borel sigma-algebra. ([[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], [[thm-measure-uniqueness-on-a-sigma-finite-pi-system]], [[thm-rational-box-generators-of-the-borel-sigma-algebra-on-rn]])

[L4] $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)=\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)$. Continuous real functions are Borel measurable by the inverse-image sigma-algebra argument. ([[thm-borel-products-of-euclidean-spaces-are-euclidean-borel]])

[L5] Under the supplied box-volume measure contract, compact bounded Borel Riemann integrals equal the corresponding measure integrals, without a choice premise. ([[lem-gaussian-density-integrals-for-supplied-length-measures]])

[L6] Continuous functions on compact Jordan sets are Riemann integrable. ([[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]])

[L7] Monotone convergence computes the nonnegative Lebesgue integral from increasing cutoffs, and every compact Jordan exhaustion computes the nonnegative improper multiple integral. ([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[thm-nonnegative-improper-multiple-integral-by-exhaustion]])

[L8] Nonnegative square roots are unique. ([[thm-of-square-roots]])

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Put $h(x)=e^{-x^2}$ and $H(x,y)=h(x)h(y)$. These continuous nonnegative functions are Borel and product-measurable by [L4]. The supplied $\lambda_1$ has the explicit finite-mass exhaustion $(-n,n]$, of measure $2n$. By [L3] its product measure exists; by [L4] it is a Borel measure on $\mathbb R^2$. Denote it $\lambda_2$; its half-open box volumes are the usual areas by the rectangle formula. Tonelli [L1] therefore gives, in the nonnegative extended sense,
$$I^2=\int_{\mathbb R}\int_{\mathbb R}H(x,y)\,dy\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R^2}H\,d\lambda_2.$$
The plane measure is thus supplied by the generic product theorem from the given length measure. [given, L1, L3, L4, construct]

2.1 Let $Q_n=[-n,n]^2$, $n\ge1$. The continuous $H$ is bounded and Riemann integrable on each compact Jordan box by [L6], and its box supplied-measure integral equals its box Riemann integral by [L5]. The nonnegative measurable cutoffs $H\mathbf1_{Q_n}$ increase to $H$. By [L7], the plane Lebesgue integral is the limit of these box integrals. The same $Q_n$ form a compact Jordan exhaustion of $\mathbb R^2$, so [L7] identifies that limit with the nonnegative improper plane integral. This is $\pi$ by [L2]. [step 1.1, L2, L4, L5, L6, L7, construct]

3.1 Steps 1.1 and 2.1 give $I^2=\pi<\infty$, so $I$ is finite. Since $I\ge0$, uniqueness of the nonnegative square root in [L8] yields $I=\sqrt\pi$. This proves the Lebesgue identity; step 2.1 explicitly supplies the bridge from the polar supplier's improper integral. [step 1.1, step 2.1, L8] ∎

## Objective

This page separates the full-data inferential target from changes introduced by algorithms, summaries, asymptotic approximations, and numerical computation. It defines a fixed-data posterior only after a measurable likelihood version and finite positive evidence have been supplied, then places that target in a declared metric space with a finite approximation chain.

Identifiability is a property of the full sampling laws: equal laws must give equal values of the estimand. The examples show that this property does not prevent a summary from discarding information, a positive ABC tolerance from changing the conditional target, a mean-field ELBO optimizer from losing correlation, a Gaussian synthetic likelihood from changing a posterior, or a local Laplace mode from missing another global mode. The total-variation expectation bounds use the event-supremum convention: factor two for functions bounded in absolute value by $M$, and the sharper $M$ bound for nonnegative functions between $0$ and $M$.

For scalar chains, the pathwise signed identity is exact. For probability laws or other objects, the metric theorem gives a triangle bound only when every adjacent comparison uses the same metric on the same space. Neither result supplies independence, variance addition, global optimizer convergence, posterior consistency, or calibration. In particular, a model's identifiability does not imply that an approximation procedure preserves its exact inferential target.


The Gaussian mean-field calculation takes its reference area measure as supplied and obtains the needed length measure from a fixed unit-height strip. A local Darboux comparison proves its density normalizers and moments without adding a choice axiom or constructing those measures.

## Examples

The examples use the exact target and metric conventions from the companion A page. They isolate five distinct mechanisms: local curvature overlooks a second posterior mode; optimizing within a mean-field family can lose dependence; matching only Gaussian summary moments can change a synthetic-likelihood posterior; a nonconstant summary can have a parameter-independent law; and positive tolerance changes even an identity-summary target.

All finite probability calculations give explicit sample spaces, probability weights, priors, observed data, acceptance events, and posterior normalizers. ABC rejection output is identified with its tolerance-conditioned target only under the supplier theorem's IID premise and positive-acceptance condition. The Laplace example assumes Countable Choice through its Gaussian and Lebesgue change-of-variables suppliers; its total-variation comparison concerns the full posterior and a single-mode Gaussian on the common real parameter space.


The Gaussian mean-field example uses its supplied reference area measure and its induced length measure; its compact Darboux and Gaussian moment calculations add no choice axiom.
